title: UX Design Fundamentals: Professional Practice
subtitle: Diagnose, measure and fix real usability problems, then sell and lead UX work with evidence a client or team will trust.
description: An advanced, practice-heavy course for people who already know the basic UX process and want to work at a professional level. You will connect design to business metrics, apply cognitive science and African-context constraints, run card sorts, tree tests and measured usability studies, and deliver a client-ready UX audit with pricing, contracts and data protection handled properly.
outcomes: Diagnose a product funnel and set HEART metrics with targets for a UX improvement
Justify design decisions with Hick's law, Fitts's law, recognition over recall and WCAG 2.2 target sizes
Design for low bandwidth, unreliable networks, shared phones and USSD
Choose research methods and run card sorts, tree tests and SUS-scored usability tests
Synthesise research into insights and a RICE-ranked backlog
Deliver, price and lead a UX audit with severity-rated findings and NDPA-compliant research data
audience: Women who have completed an introductory UX course or work near digital products and want to offer UX audits, research and design leadership professionally.
tools: Smartphone (an Android phone is ideal for testing typical user conditions)
Laptop or desktop with Chrome for PageSpeed Insights and DevTools
Google Sheets or Excel for funnels, RICE and SUS calculations
Google Forms for surveys and simple tree tests
Figma (free plan) or paper for flows and wireframes
Optional: OptimalSort, Treejack or UXtweak free trials for card sorting and tree testing

modules.title: UX Foundations for Professionals: Outcomes, Cognition and Context
modules.overview: This module moves you past 'make it look nice' into the three foundations senior UX practitioners stand on: measurable business outcomes, the cognitive science behind usable interfaces, and the real conditions of African users (data cost, shared phones, USSD). Every lesson ends with a piece of analysis you will reuse in the capstone.

lessons.title: UX as measurable outcomes: funnels, task success and the HEART framework
objectives: Distinguish UX, UI and usability in precise professional language
Calculate step and overall conversion in a product funnel and find the biggest leak
Translate a vague goal into Goals, Signals and Metrics using Google's HEART framework
Estimate the value of a UX improvement before any design work starts

blocks.text: **User experience (UX)** is everything a person goes through when they try to get something done with a product: finding it, learning it, using it, recovering from mistakes, and getting help. The term was popularised by cognitive scientist **Don Norman**, who used it as a job title at Apple in the 1990s because 'usability' and 'interface' felt too narrow. **UI (user interface)** is the part you can see and touch: screens, buttons, text. **Usability** is one quality of UX: how easily a specific user can complete a specific task.

At an advanced level, clients and product teams will not pay for 'better UX' as an opinion. They pay for a change in a number they care about: more completed sign-ups, fewer support calls, more repeat purchases. Your first professional habit is to connect every design question to a measurable behaviour.

blocks.name: growth-analytics
blocks.alt: A person reviewing growth charts on a large screen
blocks.caption: Professional UX work starts from the numbers that show where users struggle.

blocks.text: Reading a funnel

A **funnel** lists the steps users must pass through to reach a goal, with the number of people who reach each step. **Step conversion** is people at a step divided by people at the step before. **Overall conversion** is people who finish divided by people who started. The step with the lowest conversion is usually your biggest leak, and the best place to research first.

blocks.title: Worked example: finding the leak in a savings app onboarding
blocks.context: For example, Amaka is a UX consultant hired by a small Lagos savings app. The founder says 'onboarding is bad'. Amaka asks for last month's analytics instead of opinions.
steps: Downloads: 10,000. Started sign-up: 6,200. Passed BVN (Bank Verification Number) check: 3,100. Funded wallet: 2,480.
Overall conversion: 2,480 / 10,000 = 24.8%. The BVN step loses half of everyone who reaches it, so it is the leak.
She models a realistic goal: if research-led fixes raise the BVN step from 50% to 65%, then 6,200 x 0.65 = 4,030 pass, and 4,030 x 0.80 = 3,224 fund their wallet.
Difference: 3,224 minus 2,480 = 744 extra funded users a month, with no extra marketing spend.
blocks.result: Amaka's proposal now says 'investigate and redesign the BVN step, target 65% step conversion', which the founder can check later. Her research plan focuses on why people stop at that step: missing BVN, fear of sharing it, or errors in the form.

blocks.title: Numbers show where, not why
blocks.text: Analytics tell you where people leave. They never tell you why. Always pair a funnel with qualitative research such as interviews or usability tests before you redesign anything.
The HEART framework

Researchers at Google published **HEART** as a way to choose user-centred metrics for large products. It has five categories. You do not need all five for every project; pick the ones that match the product goal.

head: Category
What it captures
Example metric for a savings app
rows: Average score on a short in-app survey after funding
How much and how often people use it
Deposits per active user per month
New users or new users of a feature
Share of new users who set up an automatic weekly save
Share of last month's savers who saved again this month
Completion rate and median time for the BVN step

blocks.text: HEART comes with a simple process called **Goals, Signals, Metrics**. A **goal** is what the product wants for users in plain words. A **signal** is a behaviour or attitude that would show the goal is being met. A **metric** is the exact number you will track, with a time window. Add a **target** so everyone knows what 'better' means.

blocks.title: From vague goal to trackable metric
items: Goal: users finish onboarding
Signal: BVN step completed
Metric: step conversion weekly
Target: 50% to 65%
blocks.caption: Each arrow forces the team to be more specific until the goal can be measured.

blocks.text: Task-level measures you will use all course

items: **Effectiveness**: did they complete the task? (completion rate)
**Efficiency**: how long did it take, how many steps or taps? (time on task, clicks)
**Errors**: how many mistakes, and could they recover?
**Satisfaction**: how did it feel? (short questionnaires, covered in Module 2)

blocks.text: Effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction come from the classic definition of usability in the ISO 9241-11 standard: the extent to which specified users can achieve specified goals in a specified context of use. Errors are usually reported alongside effectiveness. Learning the formal definition helps when you write for corporate or government clients, who often expect standard language.

blocks.title: Ask for read-only analytics access
blocks.text: In discovery, ask the client for viewer access to Google Analytics, Firebase, Mixpanel or whatever they use. Viewer access lets you read the funnel without any risk of changing their setup.

A final point on honesty: when you present an estimate like '744 extra funded users a month', label it as a projection based on stated assumptions. If the real result after release is lower, you will still have a clear baseline to learn from, and your credibility stays intact.

takeaways: UX is the whole experience; UI is the visible layer; usability is one measurable quality
Find the step with the lowest conversion first: that is where research pays off fastest
Use HEART with Goals, Signals, Metrics and a target so 'better' can be checked
Analytics show where users leave; research shows why

activity.title: Build a HEART sheet for a real product
steps: Choose an app or website you use often, for example a bank, ride-hailing or school portal.
Write the main user task in one sentence and list its funnel steps (4 to 6 steps).
Invent plausible practice numbers for each step, then calculate step and overall conversion.
Mark the biggest leak and write one Goal, one Signal, one Metric and one Target for it.
Pick two other HEART categories that matter for this product and write one metric each.
activity.evidence: A one-page sheet (Google Sheets or paper photo) with the funnel, calculations and HEART table

lessons.title: The cognitive science behind usable interfaces
objectives: Apply Hick's law and Fitts's law to real layout decisions
Calculate a Fitts's law index of difficulty to compare two button designs
Reduce memory load using recognition, chunking and familiar patterns
Check touch targets against WCAG 2.2 and platform guidelines

blocks.text: Good interface decisions are not taste. Many rest on decades of research about how people perceive, decide and move. When a developer or client asks 'why this way?', a professional can name the principle and show the evidence. This lesson covers the laws you will quote most often.

blocks.name: brain
blocks.alt: A 3D illustration of a human brain
blocks.caption: Usable design works with the limits of human attention, memory and movement.

blocks.text: Hick's law: more choices, slower decisions

**Hick's law** says the time to choose grows as the number of equally likely options grows, roughly in proportion to the logarithm of that number. In practice: a home screen with 18 equal tiles slows people down, especially first-time users. The fix is not always fewer features. Group options, put the two or three most common tasks first, and move rare tasks one level down.
Fitts's law: big and close is fast

**Fitts's law** says the time to reach a target depends on the distance to it and its size. Far and small is slow and error-prone. Near and large is fast. A common form used in HCI (human-computer interaction) is the **index of difficulty**: ID = log2(D / W + 1), measured in bits, where D is distance and W is the target's width along the direction of movement. A higher ID means a slower, harder tap.

blocks.title: Worked example: sizing a 'Pay now' button
blocks.context: For example, Zainab is reviewing a checkout screen for a phone accessories shop. The thumb rests near the bottom of the screen. The 'Pay now' button is 400 pixels away from the thumb's resting point.
steps: Current button height (the direction of movement): 48 px. ID = log2(400 / 48 + 1) = log2(9.33) = about 3.22 bits.
Option A, make it 96 px tall: ID = log2(400 / 96 + 1) = log2(5.17) = about 2.37 bits.
Option B, keep 48 px but move it to a fixed bar 120 px from the thumb: ID = log2(120 / 48 + 1) = log2(3.5) = about 1.81 bits.
Option B gives the biggest reduction and keeps the screen tidy; it also follows the familiar bottom-bar pattern.
blocks.result: Zainab recommends a sticky bottom 'Pay now' bar, full width, at least 48 px tall. She notes the reasoning so the developer understands it is not a style preference.

blocks.text: Minimum touch target sizes

head: Guideline
Minimum target
rows: WCAG 2.2, criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), level AA
24 by 24 CSS pixels, or enough spacing around smaller targets
WCAG 2.2, criterion 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), level AAA

blocks.text: Treat 24 px as the legal-style floor, and 44 to 48 as your working default on phones. Users on bumpy bus rides, people with tremors and older users with reduced vision all benefit.
Memory: recognition beats recall

Working memory is small. George Miller's famous 1956 paper is often quoted as '7 plus or minus 2', but later research suggests the practical limit is closer to about four chunks, and the number was never meant as a rule for menu length. The useful lesson is: **do not make people remember things the interface could show them.**

blocks.title: Recall versus recognition
items: Recall (harder)
Recognition (easier)
left: Remember a code from the last screen
blocks.caption: Moving tasks from the left column to the right reduces errors and support calls.

blocks.text: **Chunking** helps when people must handle long numbers. A 10-digit NUBAN account number is easier to check as 012 345 6789 than as 0123456789. Show the bank name and account name after entry so people confirm by recognition, not by re-reading digits.
Jakob's law and mental models

**Jakob's law**, named after usability expert Jakob Nielsen, says users spend most of their time on other products, so they expect yours to work the same way. A **mental model** is the user's belief about how something works. If every bank app your users know puts 'Transfer' on the home screen, hiding it in a menu breaks their model. Innovate where it adds value; follow conventions everywhere else.

blocks.title: Quote the principle, then test
blocks.text: Laws predict tendencies, not every user. Use them to make a strong first design and to explain choices, then confirm with a usability test.
Cognitive load in forms

**Cognitive load** is the mental effort a task demands. Some load is unavoidable because the task itself is complex, such as choosing a loan term. Much of it is **extraneous**, caused by the design: unclear labels, jargon, too many fields on one screen, or instructions that disappear when the user starts typing. Your job is to remove extraneous load so attention goes to the real decision.

items: Ask only for what you need now; defer optional fields until later.
Keep labels visible above fields instead of using placeholder text that vanishes.
Break long forms into short steps with a progress indicator, for example 'Step 2 of 4'.
Use sensible defaults and auto-fill, such as showing the account name automatically once a valid account number and bank are entered.

blocks.text: When you explain recommendations to developers or clients, name the principle and the expected effect in one sentence, for example: 'Larger, closer Pay button (Fitts's law) should reduce mis-taps and time to pay.' This turns design debate into testable predictions.

takeaways: Hick's law: group and prioritise choices instead of showing everything at once
Fitts's law: important targets should be large and close to where the thumb already is
Use 44 to 48 px targets on mobile; never below the WCAG 2.2 AA floor of 24 px
Design for recognition, chunk long numbers, and respect familiar patterns

activity.title: Cognitive audit of one screen
steps: Screenshot the main screen of an app you use daily.
Count the equal-weight choices on the screen and note where Hick's law applies.
Measure the main button with a ruler app or by estimate and calculate its Fitts ID from the thumb position.
Find two places where the app forces recall and rewrite them as recognition.
Write three recommendations, each naming the principle it relies on.
activity.evidence: Annotated screenshot plus a short note with your calculations and three principle-backed recommendations

lessons.title: Designing for African realities: data cost, shared phones and USSD
objectives: Set a page-weight budget and calculate its data cost for a typical user
Design offline-tolerant states for unreliable networks, especially for payments
Structure a USSD menu flow within its screen and session limits
Plan for shared devices, multiple languages and low literacy

blocks.text: Most UX guidance online is written for users with fast networks, new phones and cheap data. Many of your users will have none of these. Designing well for African conditions is a specialist skill, and it is one of the strongest things you can offer local fintech, health, agriculture and education products, and international companies entering African markets.

blocks.name: no-signal
blocks.alt: A person holding a phone with no network signal
blocks.caption: Design for the moment the network drops, not only for perfect conditions.

blocks.text: Data cost is a UX problem

Every megabyte your product downloads is paid for by the user. Heavy images, auto-playing video and large app updates make people ration their use or uninstall. A **performance budget** is a limit the team agrees in advance, such as 'the home screen must load under 1 MB on first visit'.

blocks.title: Worked example: what a heavy home page costs a user
blocks.context: For example, Tunde manages a market-price website for farmers. The current home page is 4 MB because of large photos. Users open it about 5 times a day.
steps: Current: 4 MB x 5 visits x 30 days = 600 MB a month, if nothing is cached.
He sets a budget of 800 KB by compressing photos to WebP, lazy-loading images below the fold and removing an unused font.
New: 0.8 MB x 5 x 30 = 120 MB a month, and less after caching.
Saving per user: 600 minus 120 = 480 MB a month, which is a large share of a small monthly data bundle.
blocks.result: Tunde adds the 800 KB budget to the project's definition of done, and checks it with the Network tab in Chrome DevTools or Google's PageSpeed Insights before each release.

blocks.text: Designing for unreliable networks

items: **Save progress locally**: long forms (KYC, applications) should keep what was typed if the network drops or the app closes.
**Show honest states**: loading, offline, failed, and pending must look different. A spinner that never ends is the worst state.
**Never risk double payment**: after a timeout, show 'We are checking your payment' and the real status from the server, not a 'try again' button that may charge twice.
**Use skeleton screens and text first** so people can read while images load.
**Consider a Progressive Web App (PWA)**: it can cache key screens and work offline without a large app-store download.

blocks.title: Money and trust
blocks.text: Unclear payment states are a major cause of distrust and of scams, because worried users search for 'customer care' numbers online and meet fraudsters. Always show a transaction reference, the final status, and official support channels inside the product.
USSD: designing without a screen as you know it

**USSD** (the *code# menus) works on any GSM phone without internet and is widely used for banking, airtime and mobile money. Businesses usually get a code through a licensed aggregator. The design rules are strict: the GSM standard allows at most 182 characters per screen and many networks show fewer, sessions time out quickly, there are no images, and typing is slow. Every screen is a numbered menu or a short input.

blocks.title: A cooperative contribution USSD flow
items: Dial code, see menu
1 Pay contribution
Enter amount
Confirm with PIN
Reference sent by SMS
blocks.caption: Five short screens, with the key information repeated by SMS because the USSD session disappears.

items: Put the most common task as option 1.
Keep each screen under about 160 characters to be safe across networks.
Use '0 Back' and '00 Main menu' consistently on every screen.
Confirm the amount and recipient name before asking for a PIN.
Send an SMS receipt, since the session closes and users cannot scroll back.

blocks.text: Shared phones, languages and literacy

A phone may be shared in a family or used by an agent for many customers. Offer quick logout, a PIN or biometric lock on sensitive screens, and avoid showing balances on notifications. Offer the languages your users actually speak, for example Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo or Nigerian Pidgin, and have translations checked by native speakers in context, not only by a tool. For low-literacy users, pair short text with clear icons, use audio or voice notes where possible, and test with the real audience.

head: Constraint
Design response
rows: Performance budget, compressed images, no autoplay video
Local drafts, clear offline and pending states
USSD or SMS channel for the core task
Quick logout, PIN on sensitive screens, private notifications
Language choice on first screen, native-speaker review

blocks.text: Testing in real conditions

Your own phone and office Wi-Fi hide most of these problems. Chrome DevTools lets you simulate slower networks with the throttling menu in the Network tab, and Android phones can be set to a slower network type in settings. Better still, test on a low-cost Android phone with a normal prepaid data bundle, outdoors, and in the evening when networks are busy. Ask participants to use their own phones during research sessions whenever possible, because their storage, battery and data situation is part of the experience you are studying.

Write these conditions into your research reports: device model, network type and whether the test was done on Wi-Fi or mobile data. A finding such as 'the page took over 20 seconds to show prices on 3G' only makes sense with that context.

takeaways: Data cost is part of UX: agree a performance budget and measure it
Design clear offline, failed and pending states, especially for payments
USSD screens are short numbered menus; confirm before PIN and send an SMS receipt
Plan for shared phones, local languages and low literacy from the start

activity.title: Context check of a product you know
steps: Open a website you use on your phone and check its size with PageSpeed Insights or Chrome DevTools.
Calculate its monthly data cost for a user who opens it 3 times a day.
Turn on airplane mode mid-task and screenshot what the product shows.
Write a 5-screen USSD version of its main task, counting characters on each screen.
List three changes that would make it work better for shared phones or other languages.
activity.evidence: A note with the page size, data calculation, offline screenshot, USSD script with character counts and three changes

quiz.q: A funnel shows 8,000 visitors, 4,000 start checkout and 1,000 pay. What is the step conversion from checkout start to payment?
quiz.explain: Step conversion is 1,000 divided by 4,000, which is 25%. 12.5% is the overall conversion from visitors (1,000 / 8,000).

quiz.q: A team says 'we want users to trust the app more'. In HEART's Goals, Signals, Metrics process, what should come next?
options: Name a behaviour or attitude that would show trust, then a number to track it
Add more security text to every screen
quiz.explain: After the goal comes a signal (for example more users enabling auto-save or higher trust ratings), then a precise metric with a time window and target.

quiz.q: Which change most reduces the Fitts's law difficulty of tapping 'Send'?
options: Making it smaller so it fits beside other buttons
Making it larger and moving it closer to the thumb
quiz.explain: Fitts's law depends on distance and size. Larger and closer means a lower index of difficulty and faster, more accurate taps.

quiz.q: A transfer times out on a weak network. What should the screen show?
options: 'Failed. Try again' with a retry button
A spinner until the user closes the app
'We are checking your payment' and then the real status from the server, with a reference
Nothing, and return to the home screen
quiz.explain: A blind retry can charge twice. The safe pattern is to check and display the true status with a reference the user can quote to support.

quiz.q: Why should a USSD flow send an SMS receipt at the end?
options: SMS is cheaper than USSD for the business
The USSD session closes and the user cannot scroll back to see the reference
So the user can reply to cancel
quiz.explain: USSD sessions disappear when they end. An SMS keeps the amount, recipient and reference where the user can find them later.

modules.title: Research, Synthesis and Measurement Workflow
modules.overview: Here you build the professional workflow that turns questions into evidence and evidence into decisions. You will choose the right research method, validate navigation with card sorting and tree testing, synthesise findings into a ranked backlog, and measure usability with standard scores so you can prove a redesign worked.

lessons.title: Choosing research methods, card sorting and tree testing
objectives: Place research methods on the attitudinal versus behavioural and qualitative versus quantitative map
Choose a method that fits a research question, budget and timeline
Plan and run an open card sort to learn how users group content
Analyse a tree test using success rate, directness and first clicks

blocks.text: Beginners use one method for everything, usually interviews. Professionals start from the **research question** and pick the method that can answer it. Asking people what they would do (attitudinal) and watching what they actually do (behavioural) often give different answers, and both have a place.

blocks.name: sorting-thoughts
blocks.alt: A person arranging cards and ideas into groups
blocks.caption: Card sorting shows how users naturally group the things your product offers.

blocks.text: The research methods map

The Nielsen Norman Group describes UX methods along two main dimensions. **Attitudinal versus behavioural**: what people say versus what they do. **Qualitative versus quantitative**: understanding why, from a few people in depth, versus measuring how many or how much, from many people.

blocks.title: Where common methods sit
items: Usability tests, field visits
Analytics, A/B tests, tree tests
Interviews, open card sorts
Surveys, SUS questionnaires
blocks.caption: Pick the quadrant that matches your question; strong projects usually combine two.

head: Research question
Good method
Why
rows: Why do people abandon the BVN step?
Moderated usability test plus short interviews
You need to see the struggle and hear the reason
How many users want a Pidgin option?
How do users expect our features to be grouped?
Reveals their mental model of categories
Can users find 'Loan repayment' in our new menu?
Measures findability without visual design getting in the way

blocks.text: Card sorting: learning users' categories

In a **card sort**, participants group labelled cards (features or content items) in a way that makes sense to them. In an **open** sort they also name the groups. In a **closed** sort they place cards into groups you defined. A **hybrid** sort allows both. Open sorts are best early, when you are designing navigation; closed sorts check whether a proposed structure fits.

items: Write 30 to 50 cards, one feature or content item each, using plain words users know.
Recruit participants who match your users. Nielsen Norman Group suggests around 15 participants for a reliable open card sort.
Run it remotely with a tool such as OptimalSort or UXtweak, or on paper or sticky notes in person.
Look for cards that most people put together, and for cards that are split across groups: those are your naming problems.
Draft a navigation structure (an information architecture tree) from the strongest groups.

blocks.text: Tree testing: checking if people can find things

A **tree test** shows participants only a text version of your menu hierarchy, with no visuals, and asks them to find where they would complete a task. Because it is quantitative, it needs many more participants than a usability test; several dozen is common. The key measures are **success rate** (ended at the right place), **directness** (went there without backtracking) and **first click** (the first top-level choice, which strongly predicts success).

blocks.title: Worked example: tree testing a cooperative app menu
blocks.context: For example, Halima is redesigning the menu of a cooperative society app in Kano. Top-level items are Home, Savings, Loans, Payments and Profile. One task reads: 'You want to see when your next loan repayment is due. Where would you look?'
steps: 40 people complete the tree test using Treejack from Optimal Workshop.
26 of 40 end at Loans > Repayment schedule: success rate 26 / 40 = 65%.
Only 18 of 40 got there without backtracking: direct success 18 / 40 = 45%.
First clicks: 22 chose Loans, 12 chose Payments, 6 chose Savings. The 12 who chose Payments expected 'repayments' to be a payment.
She adds a 'Loan repayments' shortcut under Payments that links to the same page, and retests with 40 new people: 34 succeed, 34 / 40 = 85%.
blocks.result: The first-click data explained the failure, and a cross-link fixed it without restructuring the whole app. Halima reports both rates and the first-click split in her findings.

blocks.title: Low-budget versions
blocks.text: No paid tools? Run a card sort with paper cards at a cooperative meeting, photograph each result, and tally pairs in Google Sheets. A rough tree test can be a Google Form that shows the menu as text and asks 'Where would you click first?' for each task.

blocks.title: Consent and privacy
blocks.text: Tell participants what you are studying, how long it takes, how their answers will be used and stored, and that they can stop at any time. Collect only the personal data you need. In Nigeria this is governed by the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, covered in Module 3.
Combining methods into a plan

Strong research plans mix methods so that each covers the weakness of another. A common sequence for a navigation redesign is: interviews to understand needs, an open card sort to learn users' categories, a tree test to check the proposed structure, and finally a usability test of the designed screens. Write a one-page research plan before you start: research questions, method for each, participants and how you will recruit them, timeline, and what decision each answer will inform. If an answer would not change any decision, drop that question and save the budget.

takeaways: Start from the research question, then choose the method
What people say and what they do differ: combine attitudinal and behavioural methods
Open card sorts reveal users' categories; tree tests measure findability
Report tree tests with success rate, directness and first clicks

activity.title: Mini card sort and tree test
steps: Write 20 cards for the features of a product you know (for example a school portal).
Ask three people to sort them into groups and name each group; photograph every result.
Draft a menu tree from the strongest groups.
Write three find-it tasks and test the tree in a Google Form with at least eight people.
Calculate the success rate for each task and note the most common wrong first click.
activity.evidence: Photos of the sorts, your menu tree, and a table of task success rates and first clicks

lessons.title: Synthesis and prioritisation: from raw notes to a ranked backlog
objectives: Turn raw research notes into observations, insights and recommendations
Write user needs as job stories in the 'When, I want to, so I can' format
Map opportunities and solutions with an opportunity solution tree
Rank design ideas with the RICE scoring formula

blocks.text: Research produces a pile of notes, recordings and sticky notes. **Synthesis** is the disciplined work of turning that pile into a few clear insights that a team can act on. It is where many junior designers struggle, and where experienced designers add the most value.

blocks.name: design-objectives
blocks.alt: A designer arranging goals and objectives on a board
blocks.caption: Synthesis turns many notes into a short list of objectives the team agrees on.

blocks.text: Observation, insight, recommendation

Keep three levels separate. An **observation** is what happened, with evidence: '4 of 5 participants paused for over 20 seconds at the BVN field.' An **insight** is your interpretation of why, supported by several observations: 'Users do not know why the app needs their BVN and fear it gives access to their money.' A **recommendation** is what to change: 'Explain in one line, at the BVN field, that the number is used to confirm identity and cannot on its own be used to withdraw money.' Mixing these levels is how weak reports happen.

Do synthesis soon after sessions, while memory is fresh, and involve at least one colleague from product or engineering. People who help build the insights are far more likely to act on them. If you work alone, ask someone to challenge your groups by asking 'what evidence supports this?' for each one.
Affinity mapping

items: Write each observation on its own sticky note (or a row in a sheet), with the participant code, for example P3.
Group notes that point to the same underlying issue. Do this silently first if working in a team.
Name each group with a sentence written from the user's view, such as 'I don't trust why they want my BVN'.
Count how many participants appear in each group, not how many notes, so one talkative person does not dominate.
Turn the strongest groups into insight statements.

blocks.text: Job stories

A popular way to express needs comes from **Jobs to be Done** thinking: people 'hire' a product to make progress in a situation. A **job story** captures this: **When** [situation], **I want to** [motivation], **so I can** [expected outcome]. For example: 'When my salary arrives late in the month, I want to pause my automatic savings without penalty, so I can still pay rent on time.' Job stories focus on the situation rather than on a persona's demographics.
The opportunity solution tree

Product discovery coach Teresa Torres popularised the **opportunity solution tree**. At the top is one measurable **outcome**. Under it are **opportunities**: unmet needs and pain points from research. Under each opportunity are possible **solutions**, and under each solution are small **assumption tests** to check it before building.

blocks.title: Opportunity solution tree, top to bottom
items: Outcome: BVN step 65%
Opportunities: user pain points
Solutions: design ideas
Assumption tests: quick checks
blocks.caption: One outcome at the top keeps every idea tied to the metric the team agreed.

blocks.text: Prioritising with RICE

When you have more ideas than time, score them. **RICE**, published by the product team at Intercom, multiplies **Reach** (people affected per period) by **Impact** (3 massive, 2 high, 1 medium, 0.5 low, 0.25 minimal) by **Confidence** (100%, 80% or 50%), then divides by **Effort** (person-months). Higher scores go first.

blocks.title: Worked example: ranking three onboarding ideas
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma's team has research-backed ideas for the savings app and one quarter to work. She scores each with RICE.
steps: Idea A, save KYC form progress: Reach 3,000 users a quarter, Impact 2, Confidence 80%, Effort 2. Score = 3,000 x 2 x 0.8 / 2 = 2,400.
Idea B, add a Nigerian Pidgin language option: Reach 1,500, Impact 1, Confidence 50%, Effort 3. Score = 1,500 x 1 x 0.5 / 3 = 250.
Idea C, rewrite BVN explanation and error messages: Reach 5,000, Impact 1, Confidence 80%, Effort 0.5. Score = 5,000 x 1 x 0.8 / 0.5 = 8,000.
blocks.result: The team ships the cheap, high-reach copy fix first, then saved progress. Pidgin stays on the list with a plan to raise confidence by surveying users before investing.

blocks.title: Scores support judgement, they do not replace it
blocks.text: RICE numbers are estimates. Write down where each one came from (analytics, research counts, developer estimate) so others can challenge it, and override the score openly when there is a legal, safety or accessibility reason.
Presenting the backlog

A ranked backlog is only useful if decision makers understand it. Present it as a short table: the insight, the job story it serves, the proposed solution, the RICE score and the metric it should move. Put the top two or three items on one slide with a short clip or quote as evidence. Then agree what will be built, what will be tested first with a quick assumption test, and what is parked. Record that decision and its date in your repository, because later you will want to show which research led to which change and what happened to the metric.
Revisit the ranking after each release. New analytics or test results change Reach and Confidence, and the tree should grow and shrink as opportunities are solved or proved unimportant.

takeaways: Separate observations, insights and recommendations in every report
Count participants, not notes, when sizing an affinity group
Job stories describe the situation and motivation behind a need
Use an opportunity solution tree and RICE to choose what to build first

activity.title: Synthesise and rank
steps: Take notes from any three conversations about a product (your own interviews or tests).
Write at least 15 observations, each with a participant code.
Affinity-map them into groups and write two insight statements and two job stories.
Propose three solutions and score each with RICE, noting the source of every number.
Write the ranked list with one sentence of reasoning for the top item.
activity.evidence: Photo or sheet of your affinity map, the insight statements, job stories and RICE table

lessons.title: Measuring usability: SUS, task metrics and A/B tests
objectives: Score a System Usability Scale questionnaire correctly
Report a small-sample completion rate with an honest confidence range
Read a basic A/B test result and avoid common mistakes
Run a before-and-after measurement plan for a redesign

blocks.text: Qualitative testing tells you what to fix. **Measurement** tells you whether the fix worked and by how much. Clients trust a redesign far more when you can say 'completion rose from 3 of 8 to 7 of 8, and the usability score rose from 55 to 78' than when you say 'it feels easier'.

blocks.name: split-testing
blocks.alt: Two versions of a screen compared side by side
blocks.caption: Comparing versions with numbers shows whether a design change really helped.

blocks.text: The System Usability Scale (SUS)

SUS was created by John Brooke in 1986 and is free to use. It has 10 statements rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Odd-numbered items are positive ('I thought the system was easy to use'), even-numbered items are negative ('I found the system unnecessarily complex'). Give it right after a test session, before you discuss anything.

items: For each odd item (1, 3, 5, 7, 9), subtract 1 from the answer.
For each even item (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), subtract the answer from 5.
Add the ten results (range 0 to 40).
Multiply by 2.5 to get a score from 0 to 100. This is not a percentage.

blocks.title: Worked example: scoring one participant's SUS
blocks.context: For example, after testing a pharmacy-delivery app checkout, participant P2 answered items 1 to 10 as: 4, 2, 5, 1, 4, 2, 4, 2, 5, 1.
steps: Odd items 4, 5, 4, 4, 5 become 3, 4, 3, 3, 4. Sum = 17.
Even items 2, 1, 2, 2, 1 become 3, 4, 3, 3, 4. Sum = 17.
blocks.result: P2's SUS is 85. Average all participants' scores for the study. Published benchmarks from MeasuringU put the average SUS across many products at about 68, so 85 is well above average.

blocks.text: Task metrics and small samples

items: **Completion rate**: tasks completed without help, divided by attempts.
**Time on task**: report the median, because a few very slow users distort the mean.
**Single Ease Question (SEQ)**: after each task, 'Overall, how difficult or easy was this task?' on a 7-point scale.
**Errors**: count and describe them, and note whether the user recovered.

blocks.text: With five participants, numbers are rough. If 4 of 5 complete a task, the true rate in the wider population could be much lower. A practical method recommended by measurement specialists is the **adjusted Wald** interval: add about 2 successes and 2 failures, then calculate. Here (4 + 2) / (5 + 4) = 0.67, with a 95% margin of about 0.31, giving a plausible range of roughly 36% to 97%. Report '4 of 5' together with that range, not '80%' alone.
A/B tests

An **A/B test** sends real traffic randomly to version A (control) or B (variant) and compares a single goal metric. It needs enough users to detect a difference, a sample size decided in advance, and discipline not to stop the test the moment B looks ahead, which inflates false wins.

B is 2.5 percentage points higher, a relative lift of 2.5 / 12 = about 21%. A two-proportion test gives a p-value of about 0.02, meaning a difference this large would be unlikely if the versions truly performed the same. Use a reputable online A/B significance calculator rather than eyeballing. Small products with little traffic often cannot run valid A/B tests; use before-and-after usability testing instead.

blocks.title: Before-and-after measurement loop
items: Baseline test and metrics
Redesign the leak
Retest same tasks
Compare and report
Monitor live analytics
blocks.caption: Same tasks, same metrics, before and after: that is what makes the comparison fair.

blocks.title: Design QA before you measure
blocks.text: Before retesting, check the build against your design: empty, loading, error, offline and success states all exist, text matches, and targets are the agreed size. Measuring a broken build wastes participants.
Writing up results honestly

A professional results summary states what was measured, with whom, and how confident you are. For example: 'Five participants, recruited from current customers, tested on their own Android phones. Checkout completion rose from 2 of 5 to 5 of 5. Median time fell from 3 minutes 40 seconds to 1 minute 55 seconds. Average SUS rose from 58 to 79. With five participants these are directional results; we recommend monitoring live checkout conversion for four weeks to confirm.'

Avoid common errors: reporting SUS as a percentage, averaging SEQ scores across very different tasks, comparing results from different task wording, and claiming statistical significance from a five-person test. Keep raw data in a sheet so anyone can check your arithmetic. If a result surprises you, look at the recordings again before reporting it; the explanation is usually there.

takeaways: SUS: odd items minus 1, 5 minus even items, sum, times 2.5; about 68 is average
Report small-sample completion as counts plus a confidence range
A/B tests need traffic, a fixed sample size and no early stopping
Measure the same tasks before and after a redesign

activity.title: Run a measured mini-test
steps: Choose one task in a real app and test it with three to five people.
Record completion, time, errors and an SEQ score for each person.
Give each participant the SUS questionnaire and score it.
Calculate the median time, average SUS and an adjusted Wald range for completion.
Write a three-line summary a client could understand.
activity.evidence: A results sheet with raw answers, SUS calculations, task metrics and the three-line summary

quiz.q: A team wants to know whether users can find 'Change PIN' in a new menu before any screens are designed. Which method fits best?
quiz.explain: A tree test measures findability in a text-only hierarchy, before visual design exists. A card sort is for discovering groupings, not checking a proposed tree.

quiz.q: In a tree test, 30 of 50 people succeed and 20 of 50 succeed without backtracking. What are the success and direct success rates?
quiz.explain: 30 / 50 = 60% success and 20 / 50 = 40% direct success. Both are calculated over all 50 participants.

quiz.q: Which is an insight rather than an observation?
options: P2 tapped Back three times on the BVN screen
4 of 5 participants paused over 20 seconds at the BVN field
Users fear that sharing their BVN gives others access to their money
quiz.explain: An insight interprets why, based on several observations. The others are direct records of what happened or was said.

quiz.q: Idea X has Reach 2,000, Impact 1, Confidence 50%, Effort 1. Idea Y has Reach 1,000, Impact 2, Confidence 100%, Effort 2. Which has the higher RICE score?
quiz.explain: X = 2,000 x 1 x 0.5 / 1 = 1,000. Y = 1,000 x 2 x 1.0 / 2 = 1,000. They tie, so use judgement and evidence to decide.

quiz.q: A participant's SUS answers give a raw total of 26. What is the SUS score?
quiz.explain: Multiply the 0 to 40 total by 2.5: 26 x 2.5 = 65, slightly below the commonly cited average of about 68.

quiz.q: An A/B test is planned for 3,000 visitors per version. After 400, version B is ahead. What should the team do?
options: Continue to the planned sample size before deciding
Switch everyone to A to be safe
Restart the test with a new design
quiz.explain: Stopping early when one version looks ahead inflates false positives. Decide sample size in advance and stick to it.

modules.title: Consulting, Leadership and a Senior Portfolio
modules.overview: This module prepares you to sell, run and lead UX work. You will run a client UX audit with severity-rated findings, price and contract a project responsibly under Nigerian data protection law, and lead critiques and research knowledge in a team, then present it all as senior-level portfolio evidence.

lessons.title: Running a client UX audit: discovery, severity ratings and the findings report
objectives: Run a stakeholder discovery session that sets goals, metrics and constraints
Scope an audit around three to five critical user tasks
Rate usability problems with Nielsen's 0 to 4 severity scale
Write findings that link evidence, principle, severity and recommendation

blocks.text: A **UX audit** is a focused review of an existing product that finds the usability problems costing the business most, and recommends fixes in priority order. It is one of the best first offers for a consultant: clearly scoped, fast to deliver, and it often leads to redesign work.

blocks.name: ui-analysis
blocks.alt: A person examining an interface layout closely
blocks.caption: An audit inspects real tasks in a live product and rates what blocks users.

blocks.text: Stakeholder discovery

Before touching the product, interview the people who own it: founder, product manager, a developer and, very usefully, whoever handles customer support. Aim for 30 to 45 minutes each. Your goal is to leave with a shared outcome, the tasks that matter, and the limits you must design within.

items: **Outcome**: 'If this audit succeeds, which number moves?' (sign-ups, orders, fewer support tickets)
**Users**: who are the main users, on what devices and networks, in which languages?
**Evidence**: what analytics, reviews, support logs or past research exist? Can I have viewer access?
**Known pain**: what do customers complain about most? Ask support for the top five ticket types.
**Constraints**: budget, deadline, technology, brand rules, legal or regulatory requirements
**Decision makers**: who approves recommendations, and how do they like to receive them?

blocks.text: Scope around tasks, not screens

Pick three to five **critical tasks**, such as 'place a first order' or 'track a delivery'. For each one, walk through the live product on a mid-range Android phone on a normal mobile network, recording the screen. Note every point of hesitation, confusion, error or delay, and check each step against established heuristics such as Nielsen's 10, plus accessibility basics and the African-context checks from Module 1.
Rating severity

Jakob Nielsen's widely used scale rates each problem from 0 to 4, considering three factors: **frequency** (how many users meet it), **impact** (how hard it is to overcome) and **persistence** (does it bother users once, or every time).

head: Rating
Meaning
Typical action
rows: Must fix before release or immediately

blocks.title: Use more than one evaluator
blocks.text: Different reviewers find different problems. If possible, have two or three people review independently, then merge lists and average severity ratings. Ratings from a single reviewer are less reliable.

blocks.title: Worked example: rating findings for a fashion store checkout
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka audits the checkout of an Abuja online fashion store. The owner's outcome is more completed orders. She walks through 'buy one item and pay by card or transfer' on an Android phone over a 3G connection.
steps: Finding 1: delivery fee appears only on the final payment screen. Every buyer meets it, it causes surprise and abandonment. Principle: visibility of system status. Severity 4.

Finding 2: the phone number field rejects numbers typed with spaces, and the error just says 'Invalid input'. Frequent and confusing. Principle: help users recognise and recover from errors. Severity 3.
Finding 3: product photos total about 6 MB per page on 3G. Slow for everyone, every visit. Context check: performance budget. Severity 3.
Finding 4: 'Continue' and 'Back' buttons look identical. Occasional mis-taps. Principle: consistency and standards. Severity 2.
She orders the report by severity, then by effort, and attaches a short screen recording for findings 1 and 2.
blocks.result: The owner fixes findings 1 and 2 within a week because the evidence is clear and the fixes are cheap. Chiamaka proposes a follow-up usability test to measure the change.

blocks.text: Structure of the findings report

blocks.title: UX audit from kickoff to playback
items: Stakeholder discovery
Choose critical tasks
Walk through and record
Rate severity
Report and playback meeting
blocks.caption: Each stage feeds the next, and the playback meeting turns findings into agreed actions.

items: **Summary page**: the outcome, the top three issues, and the expected benefit of fixing them.
**Findings table**: ID, task, issue, evidence (screenshot or clip), principle, severity, recommendation, rough effort.
**Quick wins**: high severity, low effort items listed together.
**Method and limits**: tasks covered, devices, number of evaluators, what was not tested.
**Next steps**: for example a usability test to confirm the biggest issues with real users.

blocks.title: Audits are expert opinion
blocks.text: An audit predicts problems; it does not prove what real users will do. Say this honestly in the report and recommend testing the highest-severity findings with users.
The playback meeting

Do not just email the report. Hold a 45 to 60 minute **playback** with the decision makers. Start with the outcome and the top three issues, show a short clip of a real struggle, then walk through quick wins and the high-severity items. End by agreeing owners and dates for each action you can, and which findings need user testing before anyone builds. Send a short written summary of those decisions the same day. Clients remember the meeting far more than the document, and a clear action list is what turns an audit into results and repeat work.

takeaways: Start every audit with stakeholder discovery and an agreed outcome
Scope around three to five critical tasks on realistic devices and networks
Rate each problem 0 to 4 using frequency, impact and persistence
A good finding links evidence, principle, severity, recommendation and effort

activity.title: Mini audit of a live checkout or sign-up
steps: Pick a Nigerian e-commerce, school or service website with an online form.
Write a one-sentence outcome and choose two critical tasks.
Walk through each task on your phone, screenshotting every problem.
Log at least six findings with principle, severity 0 to 4 and a recommendation.
Write a one-page summary listing the top three issues and two quick wins.
activity.evidence: A findings table with screenshots and a one-page summary

lessons.title: Pricing, proposals, contracts and data protection for UX projects
objectives: Calculate a sustainable day rate from income goals, costs and billable days
Price a fixed-scope UX audit with milestone payments
Write proposal and contract clauses that control scope and protect both sides
Handle research participant data in line with the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023

blocks.text: Many skilled designers struggle because they price by guesswork, accept unlimited revisions or start work without a deposit. A professional sets a rate from real numbers, sells clearly scoped packages, and puts the agreement in writing before research begins.

blocks.name: contract-signed
blocks.alt: Two people with a signed contract
blocks.caption: A clear written agreement protects your time, your client and your research participants.

blocks.text: Working out a day rate

Not every working day is billable. You spend time on sales, admin, learning and unpaid gaps between projects. Many freelancers find only about half to two thirds of their days are paid. Your rate must cover your income goal plus business costs such as laptop replacement, software subscriptions, data, power and backup power.

blocks.title: Worked example: from income goal to audit price
blocks.context: For example, Bisi is a freelance UX designer in Ibadan. All naira figures here are illustrative and approximate; use your own real numbers.
steps: Income goal for the year: 9,600,000 naira. Business costs (tools, data, power, equipment savings): 1,200,000 naira. Total needed: 10,800,000 naira.
Working days: 260 weekdays minus about 40 for public holidays, leave and sick days = 220. At 60% billable: 220 x 0.6 = 132 billable days.
Day rate: 10,800,000 / 132 = about 81,818 naira. She rounds to 82,000 naira a day.
A two-task UX audit with a five-person follow-up test is estimated at 6 days: 6 x 82,000 = 492,000 naira. Participant thank-you payments: 5 x 5,000 = 25,000 naira. Package price: 517,000 naira.
Milestones: 50% deposit (258,500), 30% on findings draft (155,100), 20% on final playback (103,400). Check: 258,500 + 155,100 + 103,400 = 517,000.
blocks.result: Bisi sells a named, fixed-price 'Checkout UX Audit' package instead of hourly work, and she knows exactly what each extra day costs if the client wants more.

blocks.text: What the proposal must say

head: Section
What to include
rows: The metric the work aims to improve, agreed in discovery
Named tasks, platforms, number of participants and evaluators
For example visual redesign, development, new features, extra tasks
Findings report, recordings or clips, playback meeting, one revision round
Dates for each milestone and what you need from the client by when
Package price, milestones, payment method, late payment terms
Extra work is quoted in writing at the day rate before it starts

blocks.title: A six-day audit timeline
items: Deposit and kickoff
Discovery interviews
Task walkthroughs
Findings draft
User test
Playback and final payment
blocks.caption: Payments are tied to visible milestones so neither side carries all the risk.

blocks.text: Contract essentials

items: **Intellectual property**: rights to deliverables pass to the client on full payment; you keep the right to show anonymised work in your portfolio if they agree.
**Confidentiality**: you will not share their data or plans; sign their NDA if reasonable.
**Revisions**: state how many rounds are included.
**Termination**: what is paid if either side stops early.
**Data protection**: who is responsible for participant data, how long you keep recordings, and how they are deleted.

blocks.text: Research data and the law

The **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023** governs how personal data is collected and used, and the **Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)** oversees it. Research recordings, names, phone numbers and opinions are personal data. Apply its core principles: have a lawful basis such as informed consent, collect only what you need, use it only for the stated purpose, keep it secure, and do not keep it longer than necessary.

items: Use a plain-language consent form that says what is recorded, why, who will see it and for how long.
Label participants P1, P2 in notes and reports; keep the name list in a separate, password-protected file.
Blur faces, phone numbers and account details in clips you share.
Store recordings in an access-controlled folder, and delete them on the date in your contract.

blocks.title: Protect yourself from payment scams
blocks.text: Do not start work without the agreed deposit. Be wary of 'clients' who overpay and ask you to refund the difference, or who send payment links asking for your card PIN or OTP. Verify transfers in your own banking app, not from a screenshot.
Choosing a pricing model

items: **Day rate**: simple and fair for open-ended work, but clients may fear an unpredictable total.
**Fixed-price package**: best for well-defined work such as audits; you carry the risk if you underestimate, so scope tightly.
**Monthly retainer**: a set number of days each month for ongoing research or design support; agree what happens to unused days.
**Value-based**: price linked to the expected business benefit; use only when you and the client trust the numbers.

blocks.text: Whichever model you use, review it after each project. Compare the days you estimated with the days you actually worked. If you regularly run over, either your estimates are too low or your scope is too loose, and both can be fixed in the next proposal. Keep a simple log of each project's estimate, actual days and final price.

takeaways: Base your day rate on income goal plus costs, divided by realistic billable days
Sell fixed-scope packages with milestone payments and a deposit
Write out-of-scope items and a change request rule into every proposal
Treat research recordings as personal data under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023

activity.title: Price and propose your first package
steps: Write your own yearly income goal and business costs (approximate).
Estimate your working and billable days and calculate your day rate.
Define a UX audit package with tasks, deliverables and days, and price it.
Split the price into three milestones and check they add up.
Draft a one-page consent form for research participants.
activity.evidence: Your rate calculation, a one-page proposal and a participant consent form

lessons.title: Leading UX: critiques, research repositories and a senior case study
objectives: Facilitate a design critique that produces actionable, goal-based feedback
Set up a simple research repository so insights are reused, not lost
Build stakeholder buy-in with evidence such as highlight clips and observation sessions
Structure a portfolio case study that shows senior-level judgement and impact

blocks.text: At senior level, your value is not only the screens you design. It is how you raise the quality of decisions across a team: running critiques that improve work, keeping research knowledge alive, and helping non-designers see users clearly. Employers and clients look for these signals in interviews and portfolios.

blocks.name: design-feedback
blocks.alt: A team giving feedback on a design on screen
blocks.caption: Well-run critiques make the whole team's work better, not only the presenter's.

blocks.text: Running a design critique

A **critique** is a structured session where designers and colleagues review work in progress against its goals. It is not a vote on taste and not an approval meeting. Assign three roles: the **presenter** explains the goal and what feedback they need; the **facilitator** keeps time and steers comments back to goals; **critiquers** give feedback.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 45-minute critique agenda
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi leads design at a Lagos health-booking startup. A designer is presenting a new appointment-booking flow.
steps: 5 minutes: presenter states the goal ('reduce booking time and errors for first-time users') and the feedback wanted ('is the date and time step clear?').
10 minutes: walkthrough of the flow on a phone, with one research finding that shaped it.
20 minutes: critique. Each comment links to the goal: 'Given the goal of fewer errors, the time picker shows times already taken, which may cause mis-taps.'
10 minutes: facilitator summarises agreed actions, owners and open questions.
Total: 5 + 10 + 20 + 10 = 45 minutes.
blocks.result: The designer leaves with three specific actions and one question to test with users, instead of a list of personal preferences.

blocks.title: Feedback that helps
blocks.text: Teach the team to frame comments as 'Given the goal of X, I noticed Y, which might cause Z.' Ask questions before suggesting solutions, and keep solving for later unless the presenter asks for ideas.
A research repository

Without a system, research findings live in someone's laptop and are forgotten in six months, so the same questions get researched again. A **research repository** stores findings in small, searchable pieces often called **nuggets**: one observation or insight, its evidence, the source study and tags.

head: Field
Example
rows: First-time users do not trust BVN requests without a reason
4 of 5 participants hesitated; clip P3 at 12:40

blocks.text: Tools range from a shared Google Sheet or Notion database to specialist platforms such as Dovetail. The tool matters less than the habit: every study adds nuggets, and every new project starts by searching the repository.

blocks.title: How a UX team learns over time
items: Research with users
Add nuggets to repository
Critique designs against insights
Ship and measure
Update nugget status
blocks.caption: Each cycle leaves the team knowing more, instead of starting from zero.

blocks.text: Building buy-in

items: Invite product managers and developers to watch at least one live test session; seeing a user struggle is more convincing than any slide.
Share 30 to 60 second highlight clips (with consent and personal details blurred) in team channels.
Present findings with the metric from discovery, so leaders see the business link.
Credit colleagues whose ideas or code solved the problem.

blocks.text: A senior case study

A junior portfolio shows finished screens. A senior case study shows **judgement**: the problem and metric, your role and the team, how you chose methods, the hard trade-offs, and the measured result. One deep case study beats five shallow ones.

items: **Context and outcome**: the product, users, and the number you aimed to move.
**Your role**: what you led, what others did.
**Research and insight**: methods chosen and why; two or three key insights with evidence.
**Decisions and trade-offs**: options considered, what you rejected and why (for example RICE scores or constraints).
**Result**: before-and-after metrics such as completion, SUS or conversion, and what you would do next.
**Leadership signals**: critiques you ran, how you involved stakeholders, what the team kept using after you.

blocks.title: Respect confidentiality
blocks.text: Get the client's permission before publishing. Remove names, logos and real numbers if required, and say so; percentages and before-and-after comparisons can often be shared when raw figures cannot.
Mentoring and growing others

Senior designers multiply their impact by helping others grow. Pair a junior colleague with you on research sessions, let them take notes and then lead one session while you observe. Review their synthesis by asking questions rather than rewriting it. Share a short reading or video each fortnight and discuss it. In interviews for senior roles, you will often be asked for an example of how you helped someone improve; keep notes of these moments as they happen so you can tell a specific story later.

Finally, keep learning in public: write short posts about what you learned from a study (without confidential details), join local design communities and meetups, and give feedback on others' work generously. Visibility built this way often leads to referrals and leadership opportunities.

takeaways: Critiques review work against goals, with clear roles and agreed actions
A research repository turns one-off studies into lasting team knowledge
Let stakeholders see users directly to build buy-in
Senior case studies show decisions, trade-offs and measured impact

activity.title: Lead and document
steps: Run a 30-minute critique of any design (yours or a public app) with two friends or colleagues using the three roles.
Record the actions agreed and one question to test.
Create a repository sheet with the five fields above and add at least six nuggets from your earlier activities.
Write the outline of one case study using the six-part structure.
activity.evidence: Critique notes, your repository sheet and the case study outline

quiz.q: During an audit, you find that every user sees the delivery fee only on the final screen, and many abandon. Which severity rating fits best?
quiz.explain: It affects every buyer, blocks the main business outcome and happens on every purchase: high frequency, impact and persistence, so 4.

quiz.q: Total yearly need is 7,200,000 naira and you expect 120 billable days. What is your day rate?
A client asks you to 'also look at the admin dashboard' halfway through a checkout audit. What should you do?
options: Do it free to keep them happy
Treat it as a change request: quote it in writing at your day rate before starting
Drop part of the checkout work to make time
quiz.explain: Your proposal's change request rule protects both sides. Extra scope is quoted and agreed in writing first.

quiz.q: Which practice best follows the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 for usability test recordings?
options: Keep all recordings forever in case they are useful
Share full recordings in a public channel for transparency
Get informed consent, use participant codes, store securely and delete on the agreed date
Record without telling participants so they behave naturally
quiz.explain: The Act's principles include a lawful basis such as consent, data minimisation, security and storage limitation.

quiz.q: In a critique, which comment is most useful?
options: Given the goal of fewer booking errors, showing taken times in the picker may cause mis-taps
Make it look more like a big company's app
quiz.explain: Good critique links an observation to the stated goal and a likely effect, so the designer can act on it.

quiz.q: What most clearly separates a senior case study from a junior one?
options: Explaining decisions, trade-offs and measured impact
quiz.explain: Senior work is judged on reasoning and results: why you chose methods and designs and what changed as a result.

finalQuiz.q: A food-delivery app has 5,000 users open the menu, 2,000 add to cart and 1,500 pay. Which step is the biggest leak?
options: You cannot tell without a survey
finalQuiz.explain: Menu to cart converts 2,000 / 5,000 = 40%; cart to payment converts 1,500 / 2,000 = 75%. The lower conversion is the bigger leak.

finalQuiz.q: Which HEART category does 'share of last month's active users who used the app again this month' measure?
finalQuiz.explain: Users coming back over time is retention. Adoption is about new users or first use of a feature.

finalQuiz.q: A designer places 'Confirm transfer' as a small link in the top corner. Which principle does this break most directly?
finalQuiz.explain: A small, distant target is slower and more error-prone to hit, which is exactly what Fitts's law describes.

finalQuiz.q: What is the WCAG 2.2 level AA minimum target size?
options: 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or enough spacing
finalQuiz.explain: Criterion 2.5.8 at AA sets 24 by 24 CSS pixels (with a spacing exception). 44 by 44 is the AAA enhanced level.

finalQuiz.q: A page is 3 MB and a user opens it 4 times a day without caching. About how much data does it use in 30 days?
finalQuiz.explain: 3 MB x 4 visits x 30 days = 360 MB.

finalQuiz.q: Which is the best USSD menu design choice?
options: Numbered options, the most common task first, and an SMS receipt at the end
Asking for the PIN before showing the amount
finalQuiz.explain: USSD has very limited characters and no images. Put the common task first, confirm before the PIN, and send an SMS because the session disappears.

finalQuiz.q: You want to discover how users naturally group 40 features before designing navigation. Which method?
finalQuiz.explain: An open card sort lets participants create and name their own groups, revealing their mental model.

finalQuiz.q: In a tree test, most failures started with the wrong first click into 'Payments'. What is a sensible first fix to test?
options: Add a clearly labelled cross-link from Payments to the target page and retest
Ignore it because success was over 50%
finalQuiz.explain: First-click data shows where users expect the item. A cross-link or relabel matched to that expectation is cheap to test.

finalQuiz.q: Which statement is a job story?
options: When my customer pays by transfer late at night, I want to confirm it without calling my bank, so I can release the order quickly
finalQuiz.explain: A job story follows 'When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome]'.

finalQuiz.q: A participant's SUS items give a total of 30 after the odd and even adjustments. What is the SUS score and how does it compare with the commonly cited average?
finalQuiz.explain: 30 x 2.5 = 75, which is above the commonly cited average of about 68.

finalQuiz.q: An audit finding says: 'Error message says Invalid input when a phone number has spaces.' Which recommendation is strongest?
options: Accept numbers with or without spaces, and if one is still invalid, say exactly what is wrong and how to fix it
finalQuiz.explain: Preventing the error and writing a specific recovery message addresses both error prevention and helping users recover.

finalQuiz.q: Your package price is 400,000 naira with a 50/30/20 milestone split. How much is the second milestone?
finalQuiz.explain: 30% of 400,000 = 120,000 naira. The deposit is 200,000 and the final payment 80,000.

capstone.title: Measured UX Audit and Improvement Project
capstone.brief: Produce a client-ready UX audit of one real product task, backed by a user flow map, a usability test with five participants scored with task metrics and SUS, severity-rated findings and a RICE-ranked set of evidence-based recommendations, packaged with a proposal and consent form as if for a paying client.
steps: Choose a real product and one critical task (for example paying school fees, booking an appointment or buying an item) and write the outcome metric you would aim to move.
Map the current user flow step by step, marking every point of friction, confusion or data-heavy load, and check it against the African-context constraints from Module 1.
Run an expert walkthrough and log at least eight findings, each with evidence, principle and a 0 to 4 severity rating.
Recruit five participants with a plain-language consent form, run a usability test of the task, and record completion, median time, SEQ and SUS for each person.
Synthesise observations into insights, write two job stories, and rank at least four recommendations with RICE.
Write the report: summary, flow map, findings table, test results with adjusted Wald ranges, ranked recommendations, method and limits.
Add a one-page proposal pricing a follow-up redesign and retest, with milestones and out-of-scope items.
evidence: User flow map with friction points marked
Findings table with at least eight severity-rated issues and screenshots
Signed or recorded consent for each of five participants, with codes P1 to P5
Results sheet with completion, median time, SEQ and SUS calculations
Affinity map, two job stories and a RICE table
Client-ready report (PDF or Google Doc) and a one-page proposal
